lesson.title: First in Line: The Preamplifier
lesson.summary: A preamplifier is a low-level gain stage placed immediately after a weak source, such as a microphone or a guitar pickup, whose job is to raise that faint signal well above the noise floor early, while presenting a high input impedance so it does not load down the delicate source in the process.
lesson.body:
Raw microphone or pickup signals are tiny, often just a few millivolts. Any noise picked up or added by later stages in a signal chain sits at a roughly fixed absolute level, regardless of how large the wanted signal was to begin with. If real gain is not applied until after some of that fixed noise has already been added, the noise gets amplified right along with the signal, and the original signal-to-noise ratio can never be recovered downstream. Getting meaningful gain in as early as possible, right at the source, is the entire purpose of a dedicated preamplifier stage.

A preamp typically begins with, or behaves very much like, a high input impedance stage similar to the voltage follower used at the front of the instrumentation amplifier earlier in this unit. A delicate source such as a condenser microphone capsule or a guitar pickup coil has meaningful internal resistance or inductance of its own, and loading it with a low-impedance input stage would both attenuate the signal and distort its high-frequency response. The same buffering principle that protected the instrumentation amplifier's inputs protects a preamp's source here.

Suppose a microphone outputs 2mV rms and the preamp gain is 40dB. Converting to a linear ratio: 10 to the power of (40/20) = 10 squared = 100. Output = 2mV times 100 = 200mV, or 0.2V rms, roughly a hundredfold jump that lifts the signal well clear of noise picked up by any following cable or circuitry, and much closer to the range subsequent stages expect to work with.

A preamp's job stops at raising voltage. It is not built to supply meaningful current, and cannot drive a loudspeaker on its own. Delivering the actual current and power needed to move a speaker cone is the job of the power amplifier, covered next.
